name: Rayleigh–Ritz: from vibrating plates to nuclei
summary: The variational bound used throughout ab initio nuclear theory (variational Monte Carlo, truncated-basis no-core shell model, Hartree–Fock references) descends from Rayleigh's quotient for the frequencies of vibrating systems and Ritz's 1909 method for elastic plates. The quantum Rayleigh–Ritz principle is the same eigenvalue minimization.

name: Pressure and shear inside the proton
summary: The gravitational form factors of the energy–momentum tensor (including the D-term) are read as a continuum-mechanics stress tensor: a radial pressure p(r) and shear force s(r) inside the proton, with von Laue's equilibrium condition ∫p r² dr = 0 and a mechanical radius. First extractions came from deeply virtual Compton scattering, and the EIC will map them.
breaks: Local 3D densities of a relativistic, recoiling bound state depend on the frame (Breit frame vs light front), and whether p(r) is a physical pressure is debated.

name: Love numbers: from Earth tides to Lambda
summary: The tidal deformability measured from GW170817's inspiral phase is built on the Love number k_2, which A. E. H. Love introduced for the elastic tidal response of the Earth. For a neutron star k_2 measures how centrally condensed the fluid is, so the measurement bounds EOS stiffness and radius.
breaks: The neutron-star k_2 is a relativistic fluid response computed from perturbed TOV equations. Crust rigidity contributes negligibly, unlike the Earth's elastic Love numbers.

name: Neutron-star crust as an elastic solid
summary: The neutron-star crust is a Coulomb crystal whose shear modulus is set by the nuclear charges and lattice spacing. Its elastic response governs starquakes and crust breaking, the largest 'mountain' that could radiate continuous gravitational waves, and the torsional shear modes proposed for magnetar-flare QPOs.

name: Heavy-ion fireballs as relativistic viscous fluids
summary: Navier–Stokes hydrodynamics, made relativistic and causal (Israel–Stewart, second order), is the standard model of the heavy-ion fireball: pressure gradients turn the almond-shaped overlap into elliptic flow v_2, and fits to v_n extract the shear viscosity much as viscous damping is measured in a classical flow. Bjorken's boost-invariant expansion is an exact similarity solution of these equations.
sources: Bjorken (1983). "Highly relativistic nucleus-nucleus collisions: The central rapidity region". *Phys. Rev. D* 27, 140. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.27.140](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.27.140)

name: QCD critical point in the liquid–gas dynamic class
summary: Near the conjectured QCD critical point the slow modes are diffusive baryon density coupled to shear flow, exactly as at a liquid–gas critical point. That places it in Hohenberg–Halperin Model H, with the same critical slowing down, divergent conductivity and bulk-viscosity peak, and fluctuating hydrodynamics is used to predict the proton-cumulant signals.
map: \tau_{\rm relax}\sim\xi^{z},\ z\approx3\ (\text{Model H, as for a classical liquid–gas critical point})

name: Perfect liquid: eta/s of the QGP vs ordinary fluids
summary: Shear viscosity, defined by Newton's law of viscous stress, is compared across fluids through η/s, the relativistic analogue of kinematic viscosity. The QGP sits near ħ/4πk_B, about an order of magnitude below helium, nitrogen or water at their minima, which makes it the most nearly ideal (Euler) fluid known.
breaks: Kinetic theory gives η ∼ ρ v̄ λ (mean free path), which loses meaning at strong coupling where there are no quasiparticles. The 1/4π value is a holographic result for idealized gauge theories, not a proven lower bound.
sources: Kovtun, Son & Starinets (2005). "Viscosity in Strongly Interacting Quantum Field Theories from Black Hole Physics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 94, 111601. [arXiv:hep-th/0405231](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0405231)

name: Irrotational and viscous liquid-drop fission dynamics
summary: The descent from saddle to scission is modelled as flow of an incompressible nuclear fluid. Irrotational (Werner–Wheeler) flow gives the collective inertia, and adding two-body viscosity through Navier–Stokes (Davies–Sierk–Nix) slows the descent, stretches the neck and lowers fragment kinetic energies. Measured kinetic energies and prescission neutrons calibrate the dissipation.
breaks: Nuclear dissipation is mostly one-body (nucleons hitting the moving surface), not two-body viscosity, because the nucleon mean free path is comparable to the nuclear size.

name: Convective mixing sets s- and i-process yields
summary: Neutron-capture nucleosynthesis depends on classical fluid instabilities. In AGB stars, partial mixing at convective boundaries forms the ¹³C pocket that powers the main s-process, convective-reactive ingestion of hydrogen into helium-burning zones drives the i-process, and in core-collapse supernovae Rayleigh–Taylor fingers carry fresh ⁵⁶Ni outward, as seen in SN 1987A.

name: Fission as Rayleigh's charged-drop instability
summary: Bohr–Wheeler fission is Rayleigh's instability of a charged liquid drop: surface tension restores and Coulomb repulsion drives the quadrupole mode, and the sphere loses stability when E_C = 2E_S (fissility x = 1). Because the liquid-drop barrier vanishes for the heaviest nuclei, they survive only through shell corrections, and the final neck rupture parallels Rayleigh–Plateau pinch-off.
sources: Bohr & Wheeler (1939). "The Mechanism of Nuclear Fission". *Phys. Rev.* 56, 426. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.56.426](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.56.426)
Meitner & Frisch (1939). "Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons: a New Type of Nuclear Reaction". *Nature* 143, 239. [doi:10.1038/143239a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/143239a0)

name: Heavy quarks as Brownian particles in the QGP
summary: Charm and bottom quarks (M ≫ T) random-walk through the QGP like colloids in a viscous liquid. A Langevin equation with drag and momentum diffusion, tied together by the Einstein relation, describes their thermalization, and the spatial diffusion coefficient extracted from heavy-flavour R_AA and v_2 is a key transport parameter.
breaks: Stokes drag 6πηa assumes a continuum fluid around a large sphere. The heavy quark is pointlike, comparable to the medium's interparticle spacing, and its drag comes from colour interactions with relativistic corrections, not from viscous boundary layers.

name: Jet energy loss as a wave-turbulent gluon cascade
summary: Medium-induced radiation from a jet in the QGP becomes a cascade of democratic gluon branchings. It carries energy at a constant rate from the leading parton to soft gluons and into the medium, with a Kolmogorov–Zakharov fixed-point spectrum, which explains why the lost energy reappears at large angles.
map: D(x)\propto x^{-1/2}\ (\text{KZ fixed point})\ \leftrightarrow\ E(k)\propto k^{-5/3}
breaks: The cascade is in the energy fraction x of a branching process, not in a 3D velocity field. Its flux is set by \hat q and the path length, and the inertial range ends at the medium temperature.
sources: Kolmogorov (1941; English translation 1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Turbulent cascade in early QGP thermalization
summary: Before hydrodynamics applies, the over-occupied gluon fields left by the collision thermalize through a self-similar, constant-flux energy cascade toward high momenta. This is a Kolmogorov–Zakharov-type wave turbulence (a non-thermal fixed point), the same idea as the Richardson–Kolmogorov cascade in fluids.
breaks: The cascade runs in the momentum space of weakly coupled classical gluon fields. Its exponents come from the kinetic collision term, not K41's −5/3, and there are no spatial eddies and no Navier–Stokes nonlinearity.

name: Bohr's classical stopping power
summary: Bohr's 1913 stopping theory is impulse-approximation Coulomb scattering: a fast ion passing an electron at impact parameter b gives it Δp = 2Ze²/(4πε0 b v). Integrating over b between a close-collision cutoff and the adiabatic cutoff v/ω gives the logarithmic energy loss that Bethe later made quantum, the basis of range–energy relations, Bragg peaks and detector response.

name: Rutherford scattering: a hyperbolic orbit found the nucleus
summary: Geiger–Marsden α scattering was explained by classical hyperbolic orbits in a repulsive 1/r potential. Rutherford's cross section is also exact in quantum mechanics, deviations from it still show where the nuclear force begins (closest approach, Coulomb barrier), and for heavy ions with Sommerfeld parameter η ≫ 1 classical trajectories stay quantitative.

name: Shell structure from closed classical orbits
summary: By Bertrand's theorem only the oscillator and Kepler potentials have every bound orbit closed, and that classical degeneracy is why the oscillator gives large shell gaps at 2, 8, 20, 40. In realistic wells, periodic-orbit theory (Balian–Bloch, Strutinsky, the Gutzwiller trace formula) writes the oscillating level density, the shell correction behind magic numbers and superheavy stability, as a sum over the shortest closed orbits.
map: \delta g(E)=\sum_{\rm po}A_{\rm po}\cos\left(\frac{S_{\rm po}}{\hbar}-\sigma_{\rm po}\frac\pi2\right),\ S_{\rm po}=\oint\mathbf p\cdot d\mathbf q
breaks: Spin–orbit coupling, essential for the magic numbers 28, 50, 82 and 126, needs spin-dependent extensions of the trace formula.
sources: Mayer (1949). "On Closed Shells in Nuclei. II". *Phys. Rev.* 75, 1969. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.75.1969](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.75.1969)

name: Neutron moderation by elastic-collision kinematics
summary: Slowing fission neutrons to thermal energy is pure two-body elastic-collision kinematics. Momentum and energy conservation fix the maximum fractional energy loss on a nucleus of mass number A and the mean logarithmic decrement ξ, which is why light nuclei moderate best: about 18 collisions on hydrogen against about 115 on carbon to go from 2 MeV to 0.025 eV.

name: Neutrino invented to save conservation laws
summary: The continuous β spectrum, together with the spin–statistics bookkeeping of the nuclei, seemed to break conservation of energy and angular momentum, and Bohr considered giving up energy conservation. Pauli instead postulated a light neutral spin-½ particle, which Fermi built into his theory of β decay: a conservation law predicting a particle.
map: Q=T_e+T_{\bar\nu}+T_{\rm rec},\ \textstyle\sum\mathbf p=0,\ \Delta J\ \text{balanced only with a spin-}\tfrac12\ \bar\nu
sources: Fermi (1934). "Versuch einer Theorie der β-Strahlen. I". *Z. Phys.* 88, 161. [doi:10.1007/BF01351864](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01351864)

name: Chadwick weighed the neutron with collision kinematics
summary: Chadwick identified the neutron by comparing the maximum recoil velocities of hydrogen and nitrogen nuclei struck by the unknown radiation. Head-on elastic-collision kinematics gave a neutral particle with about the proton's mass, and ruled out the γ-ray hypothesis, which needed implausibly high photon energies.
sources: Chadwick (1932). "Possible Existence of a Neutron". *Nature* 129, 312. [doi:10.1038/129312a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/129312a0)

name: Neutron-star masses from binary orbits
summary: Every neutron-star mass that constrains the EOS comes from binary celestial mechanics: Keplerian elements and the mass function, plus post-Keplerian effects (periastron advance, Shapiro delay) to break degeneracies. Demorest et al. used the Shapiro delay to measure a 2 M_⊙ pulsar, which rules out soft EOSs.
sources: Demorest et al. (2010). "A two-solar-mass neutron star measured using Shapiro delay". *Nature* 467, 1081. [doi:10.1038/nature09466](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09466)

name: Vortical fireball: spin polarization from rotation
summary: Off-central collisions carry enormous orbital angular momentum, and the fluid's thermal vorticity (about 10^22 s^-1, the most vortical fluid known) polarizes Λ hyperons along it. The equilibrium density matrix is the rotating-frame one, so spin aligns with ω as in the Barnett effect.

name: r-modes: Coriolis-restored waves that spin stars down
summary: The r-modes of a rotating star are Rossby waves with the Coriolis force as their restoring force. Gravitational radiation drives them unstable (Chandrasekhar–Friedman–Schutz) unless the shear and bulk viscosity of dense matter damp them, so the observed spins of fast pulsars constrain neutron-star viscosity and composition.

name: Cranking model: nuclei in the rotating frame
summary: Inglis's cranking model solves the nucleon problem in a frame rotating at ω. Its Routhian H' = H − ωJ_x contains the Coriolis and centrifugal terms and yields moments of inertia, and the Coriolis force breaking high-j pairs and aligning their spins explains backbending in yrast bands.
map: H'=H-\omega J_x,\ \mathcal I^{(1)}=\frac{\langle J_x\rangle}{\omega}\ \leftrightarrow\ \mathbf F_{\rm Cor}=-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v

name: Rotating-drop shape bifurcations (Maclaurin–Jacobi)
summary: A rotating charged liquid drop follows the classical sequence of rotating fluid masses. Oblate axisymmetric shapes bifurcate into triaxial Jacobi-like shapes at a critical angular momentum, and the fission barrier vanishes at higher spin. Cohen, Plasil and Swiatecki mapped these sequences for nuclei, and a Jacobi shape transition has been reported in hot, fast-rotating nuclei through GDR splitting.
breaks: Surface tension replaces self-gravity, so the sequences differ quantitatively from the Maclaurin–Jacobi ones. Quantized angular momentum, shell effects (superdeformed bands) and pairing modify the classical drop.

name: Wall-formula dissipation needs chaotic nucleon billiards
summary: One-body dissipation treats nucleons as a gas bouncing inside a moving container (the wall-and-window formula of Błocki, Swiatecki and co-workers). Classical billiard simulations showed that the full wall-formula damping holds only when particle motion in the container shape is chaotic and is much weaker for integrable shapes, which ties fission damping to classical chaos.
map: \dot E=\rho\bar v\oint\dot n^2\,dS\ (\text{full strength only for chaotic billiards})

name: Compound-nucleus resonances and quantum chaos
summary: Neutron-resonance spacings in compound nuclei (the Nuclear Data Ensemble) follow the Wigner–Dyson GOE statistics that Wigner introduced for nuclei. The Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit conjecture ties such spectra to classically chaotic Hamiltonian dynamics, while regular (KAM-integrable) systems give Poisson statistics, so the 'forgetting' assumed by Bohr's compound nucleus and Hauser–Feshbach theory is an ergodicity statement.

name: Skyrmions: baryons as topological solitons
summary: In the Skyrme model, which the large-N_c limit of QCD motivates, the chiral pion Lagrangian supports stable topological solitons whose winding number is baryon number. Nucleons, nuclei and nuclear matter appear as classical field configurations quantized through their collective rotations, carrying the soliton idea from classical nonlinear waves into the strong force.
breaks: Skyrmions are topological solitons, not integrable ones: there is no inverse scattering and they deform when they interact. The model overbinds light nuclei and has been superseded quantitatively by chiral EFT.

name: Surface vibrations: Rayleigh drop modes quantized
summary: Quadrupole and octupole phonons in vibrational nuclei are the quantized normal modes of a charged liquid drop's surface, R(θ,φ) = R_0[1 + Σ α_λμ Y_λμ]. The restoring constant combines surface tension and Coulomb terms as in Rayleigh's capillary-oscillation analysis, which predicts two-phonon 0+, 2+, 4+ triplets near 2ħω.
breaks: Measured mass parameters exceed irrotational-flow values, many supposedly vibrational nuclei miss the harmonic two-phonon pattern, and shell structure rather than surface tension sets most low-lying collectivity.
sources: Weizsäcker (1935). "Zur Theorie der Kernmassen". *Z. Phys.* 96, 431. [doi:10.1007/BF01337700](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01337700)

name: Superdeformation from 2:1 oscillator resonance
summary: In the deformed (Nilsson) oscillator, whenever ω_⊥:ω_z is a ratio of small integers the classical orbits close into Lissajous figures and the quantum levels bunch into degenerate shells. The 2:1 resonance produces the superdeformed magic numbers and 3:1 gives hyperdeformation, the same commensurability that makes classical oscillator orbits periodic.

name: Giant resonances as acoustic modes of nucleon fluids
summary: In the giant dipole resonance protons oscillate against neutrons. Goldhaber–Teller model it as two rigid spheres sloshing (E ∝ A^{-1/6}), Steinwedel–Jensen as a standing sound wave of isovector density in a fixed sphere (E ∝ A^{-1/3}), and the data interpolate between them; the isoscalar monopole breathing mode measures nuclear incompressibility.
map: E_{\rm SJ}\propto A^{-1/3},\ E_{\rm GT}\propto A^{-1/6};\ E_{\rm GMR}=\hbar\sqrt{K_A/(m\langle r^2\rangle)}
breaks: Nuclear sound is zero sound of a Fermi liquid (Fermi-surface distortion at ωτ ≫ 1), not collisional first sound, and the resonances are Landau-damped into particle–hole states.

name: Wobbling: quantized precession of a triaxial top
summary: A triaxial nucleus with three distinct moments of inertia is a quantum asymmetric top. Bohr–Mottelson wobbling is the quantized small-amplitude precession of the rotation axis about the axis of largest inertia, the stable branch of Euler's tennis-racket analysis, and wobbling bands have been seen in odd-A Lu isotopes.
map: \omega_{\rm wob}=\omega_{\rm rot}\sqrt{\frac{(\mathcal I_1-\mathcal I_2)(\mathcal I_1-\mathcal I_3)}{\mathcal I_2\mathcal I_3}}\ \leftrightarrow\ \text{Euler small-oscillation frequency}
breaks: The moment hierarchy is set by quantum (irrotational-like) flow. An aligned high-j quasiparticle (transverse wobbling) changes the classical stability criterion, and some wobbling assignments are disputed.

name: Neutron-star moment of inertia and glitches
summary: Pulsar spin-down, glitches and binary spin–orbit precession are rotational dynamics of a two-component body. A glitch transfers angular momentum from a superfluid component to the crust, so the crust's share of the moment of inertia constrains the EOS, and EOS-insensitive I–Love–Q relations tie the moment of inertia to tidal deformability and quadrupole.
sources: Lattimer & Prakash (2001). "Neutron star structure and the equation of state". *Astrophys. J.* 550, 426. [arXiv:astro-ph/0002232](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0002232)

name: Rotational bands: the quantized rotor and its inertia
summary: Deformed nuclei show bands E_J = ħ²J(J+1)/2𝓘, the spectrum of a quantized free rotor with E(4+)/E(2+) = 10/3. The moment of inertia is the classical quantity, and its measured value, which lies between the irrotational-flow and rigid-body values, directly probes nuclear superfluidity.
map: E_J=\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mathcal I}J(J+1)\leftrightarrow T=\frac{L^2}{2I},\quad \mathcal I_{\rm irr}<\mathcal I_{\rm exp}<\mathcal I_{\rm rig}
breaks: There is no collective rotation about a symmetry axis (quantum indistinguishability). 𝓘 is far from rigid: pairing reduces it to roughly 30–50% of the rigid value, and it changes with spin (Coriolis anti-pairing, backbending).

name: Onsager quantization of cyclotron orbits
summary: Quantum oscillations follow from Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization of semiclassical cyclotron orbits on the Fermi surface: the action variable of the orbit fixes allowed k-space areas, so dHvA and SdH frequencies measure extremal Fermi-surface cross sections.
map: J=\oint p\,dq=2\pi\hbar(n+\gamma)\Rightarrow A_k=\frac{2\pi eB}{\hbar}(n+\gamma),\ \Delta(1/B)=\frac{2\pi e}{\hbar A_F}
sources: Onsager (1952). "Interpretation of the de Haas-van Alphen effect". *Phil. Mag.* 43, 1006. [doi:10.1080/14786440908521019](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786440908521019)

name: Berry curvature deforms semiclassical phase space
summary: Semiclassical Bloch electrons with Berry curvature obey non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics: the anomalous velocity appears and Liouville's phase-space volume is not conserved unless weighted by (1+e B.Omega/hbar), which corrects the density of states.
map: \dot{\mathbf r}=\frac1\hbar\nabla_{\mathbf k}E-\dot{\mathbf k}\times\boldsymbol\Omega,\ \hbar\dot{\mathbf k}=-e(\mathbf E+\dot{\mathbf r}\times\mathbf B);\ D=1+\frac e\hbar\mathbf B\cdot\boldsymbol\Omega
sources: Xiao, Shi & Niu (2005). "Berry Phase Correction to Electron Density of States in Solids". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 95, 137204. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.137204](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.137204)

name: Continuum mechanics of soft materials
summary: Soft matter is described at long wavelengths by continuum theories (viscoelastic fluids, gels, nematic hydrodynamics, granular rheology) built on the conservation laws and constitutive-relation framework of continuum mechanics.

name: Dislocations as topological defects of elastic crystals
summary: Plastic deformation of crystals proceeds by motion of dislocations, line defects labelled by a Burgers vector, whose long-range stress fields are solutions of continuum elasticity; their unbinding drives KTHNY two-dimensional melting.
map: \oint d\mathbf u=\mathbf b;\ \sigma_{\text{screw}}=\frac{\mu b}{2\pi r};\ \tau_{\text{Peierls}}\ll\mu/30\ (\text{ideal strength})
sources: Taylor (1934). "The mechanism of plastic deformation of crystals. Part I.—Theoretical". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 145, 362. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1934.0106](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1934.0106)

name: Elastic waves as long-wavelength acoustic phonons
summary: Acoustic phonon branches at small k are the elastic waves of continuum elasticity: their slopes are the longitudinal and transverse sound speeds fixed by elastic constants, which phonon dispersion measurements determine.

name: Contact mechanics, force chains and the Janssen effect
summary: Static granular packs transmit stress through heterogeneous force chains between Hertzian contacts; frictional wall support saturates pressure with depth in silos (Janssen effect), so granular stress cannot be treated as hydrostatic.
sources: Jaeger, Nagel & Behringer (1996). "Granular solids, liquids, and gases". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 68, 1259. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.68.1259](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.68.1259)

name: Maxwell counting and isostatic jamming
summary: Maxwell's 1864 constraint counting for the rigidity of frames gives the isostatic contact number z=2d at the jamming transition; above jamming, shear modulus and excess contacts grow as power laws of compression.
sources: Maxwell (1864). "On the calculation of the equilibrium and stiffness of frames". *Phil. Mag.* 27, 294. [doi:10.1080/14786446408643668](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786446408643668)
Liu & Nagel (1998). "Jamming is not just cool any more". *Nature* 396, 21. [doi:10.1038/23819](https://doi.org/10.1038/23819)

name: Frank orientational elasticity and liquid-crystal elastomers
summary: Frank theory is an elasticity for the director field (splay, twist, bend) instead of displacements; coupling it to a rubber network gives liquid-crystal elastomers with 'soft elasticity' and large reversible actuation.
breaks: The director is a unit headless vector, so Frank elasticity has topological defects and no restoring force for uniform rotations; a fluid nematic has zero shear modulus, unlike a solid.

name: Rubber elasticity: entropic springs to neo-Hookean solids
summary: Each network strand is an entropic Gaussian spring, so averaging over strands gives the neo-Hookean strain-energy function of finite-strain continuum elasticity with shear modulus n k_B T, explaining why rubber stiffens on heating.
sources: Treloar & Montgomery (1949). "The physics of rubber elasticity". *Phys. Today*. [doi:10.1063/1.3060678](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3060678)

name: Topological mechanics of isostatic lattices
summary: Band topology applied to the compatibility matrix of Maxwell (isostatic) lattices predicts floppy zero modes localized on particular edges, an index theorem for mechanical metamaterials analogous to the SSH chain.
map: N_0-N_S=dN-N_B;\ \text{topological polarization }\mathbf R_T=\sum_i n_i\mathbf a_i\ (\text{winding of }\det C(\mathbf k))
sources: Kane & Lubensky (2014). "Topological boundary modes in isostatic lattices". *Nat. Phys.* 10, 39. [arXiv:1308.0554](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.0554)

name: Electron hydrodynamics in graphene
summary: When electron-electron collisions dominate over impurity and phonon scattering, electrons in clean graphene flow as a viscous fluid obeying Navier-Stokes-like equations, producing negative nonlocal resistance from backflow whirlpools and Poiseuille profiles.
sources: Bandurin et al. (2016). "Negative local resistance caused by viscous electron backflow in graphene". *Science* 351, 1055. [doi:10.1126/science.aad0201](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad0201)

name: mu(I) rheology: granular matter as a viscoplastic fluid
summary: Dense granular flows obey a local friction law in which the effective friction depends on the inertial number; inserted into continuum momentum equations it predicts flows on inclines, in silos and in rotating drums.
sources: Jop, Forterre & Pouliquen (2006). "A constitutive law for dense granular flows". *Nature* 441, 727. [doi:10.1038/nature04801](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04801)

name: Nematodynamics: anisotropic viscous flow
summary: Ericksen-Leslie theory couples the Navier-Stokes equations to director rotation, giving three Miesowicz viscosities, flow alignment and backflow; it controls display switching times and active-nematic hydrodynamics.
sources: Leslie (1968). "Some constitutive equations for liquid crystals". *Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal.* 28, 265. [doi:10.1007/BF00251810](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00251810)

name: Electroconvection in nematics
summary: Above a threshold voltage nematic layers develop convection rolls (Williams domains) through the Carr-Helfrich mechanism, an anisotropic analogue of Rayleigh-Benard convection and a classic system for pattern formation and spatiotemporal chaos.
sources: Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Colloids, polymers and swimmers in Stokes flow
summary: Soft-matter dynamics is overdamped: colloid diffusion, polymer Rouse-Zimm dynamics and microswimming are governed by Stokes drag and long-range hydrodynamic interactions (Oseen tensor).
map: \mathbf F=6\pi\mu a\mathbf U,\ \mathsf O(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{8\pi\mu r}(\mathbb 1+\hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r})

name: Microswimmers at low Reynolds number
summary: Bacteria and synthetic swimmers live at Re~1e-5, where Purcell's scallop theorem forbids reciprocal strokes and Stokesian far fields (pusher/puller force dipoles) set their collective hydrodynamics and active stresses.
map: \mu\nabla^2\mathbf u=\nabla p,\ \mathbf u_{\text{dipole}}\propto\frac{p}{8\pi\mu r^2}[3(\hat{\mathbf e}\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})^2-1]\hat{\mathbf r}
sources: Marchetti et al. (2013). "Hydrodynamics of soft active matter". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 85, 1143. [arXiv:1207.2929](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.2929)

name: Stokes drag and diffusion of colloids
summary: Colloid diffusion follows from Stokes drag via the Einstein relation, and sedimentation, hydrodynamic interactions and lubrication forces between colloids are low-Reynolds-number flow problems.

name: Active turbulence versus inertial turbulence
summary: Dense bacterial suspensions and active nematics show chaotic mesoscale vortices with power-law energy spectra at Reynolds numbers far below 1, driven by active stress rather than inertia.
map: E(k)\sim k^{-5/3}\ (\text{Kolmogorov, inertial})\ \text{vs}\ E(k)\ \text{power laws set by active length }\ell_a=\sqrt{K/|\zeta|}
breaks: Energy is injected at every scale by active stress and dissipated by viscosity, with no inertial cascade; the vortex size is set by an active length, and spectral exponents are not universal.
sources: Wensink et al. (2012). "Meso-scale turbulence in living fluids". *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.* 109, 14308. [doi:10.1073/pnas.1202032109](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1202032109)

name: Polymer drag reduction and elastic turbulence
summary: Dilute long polymers reduce turbulent drag by up to ~80% (Toms effect) by suppressing near-wall vortices, and in viscous flows polymer elasticity alone drives chaotic 'elastic turbulence' at Reynolds numbers far below 1.
sources: Groisman & Steinberg (2000). "Elastic turbulence in a polymer solution flow". *Nature* 405, 53. [doi:10.1038/35011019](https://doi.org/10.1038/35011019)

name: Inelastic collisions and granular gases
summary: Grains collide with a restitution coefficient below 1, so a granular gas loses energy in every collision; the resulting homogeneous cooling (Haff's law) and clustering instability follow from momentum conservation with kinetic-energy loss.
sources: Haff (1983). "Grain flow as a fluid-mechanical phenomenon". *J. Fluid Mech.* 134, 401. [doi:10.1017/S0022112083003419](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112083003419)

name: Chaotic billiards and mesoscopic conductance fluctuations
summary: Ballistic quantum dots whose classical shape gives chaotic trajectories show universal conductance fluctuations and weak-localization lineshapes governed by random-matrix theory, while regular (integrable) shapes do not; classical chaos thus controls quantum transport statistics.
sources: Marcus et al. (1992). "Conductance fluctuations and chaotic scattering in ballistic microstructures". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 69, 506. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.506](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.506)

name: Frenkel-Kontorova model and the standard map
summary: Ground states of the Frenkel-Kontorova model of an incommensurate adsorbate or modulated crystal correspond to orbits of an area-preserving twist map; Aubry's pinning transition, where the incommensurate phase locks to the lattice, is the breakup of a KAM torus, and the devil's staircase of commensurate phases follows.
sources: Aubry (1983). "The twist map, the extended Frenkel-Kontorova model and the devil's staircase". *Physica D* 7, 240. [doi:10.1016/0167-2789(83)90129-X](https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2789(83)90129-X)

name: FPUT anharmonic lattice and the discovery of solitons
summary: The 1955 Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou simulation of an anharmonic atomic chain failed to thermalize its phonon modes; Zabusky and Kruskal's continuum limit, the KdV equation, explained the recurrence and introduced the soliton.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

name: Magnetic skyrmions as topological solitons
summary: Skyrmions are localized, particle-like solutions of the nonlinear micromagnetic field equations, stable because of an integer winding number, the topological-soliton class first introduced by Skyrme for nucleons.
sources: Nagaosa & Tokura (2013). "Topological properties and dynamics of magnetic skyrmions". *Nat. Nanotechnol.* 8, 899. [doi:10.1038/nnano.2013.243](https://doi.org/10.1038/nnano.2013.243)

name: Fluxons in long Josephson junctions are sine-Gordon solitons
summary: The phase difference along a long Josephson junction obeys the sine-Gordon equation; its kink solitons are fluxons carrying one flux quantum, which move relativistically at the Swihart velocity and underlie flux-flow oscillators.

name: SSH domain-wall solitons and topological zero modes
summary: Domain walls between the two dimerization patterns of polyacetylene are solitons that bind a mid-gap zero mode with fractional charge or reversed spin-charge relation; the SSH chain is now the prototype 1D topological insulator (Jackiw-Rebbi index).
sources: Su, Schrieffer & Heeger (1979). "Solitons in Polyacetylene". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 42, 1698. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.1698](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.1698)

name: Flocking as synchronization in space
summary: Alignment of headings in the Vicsek model is Kuramoto-like phase synchronization of self-propelled oscillators, with the twist that particles move and so couplings change; both show noise-driven order-disorder transitions.
breaks: Vicsek particles move, so the coupling network changes with the order itself, giving density bands and giant number fluctuations that have no counterpart in fixed-network Kuramoto models; their order parameter is a vector, not a phase.
sources: Vicsek et al. (1995). "Novel Type of Phase Transition in a System of Self-Driven Particles". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 75, 1226. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.1226](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.1226)

name: Synchronization of Josephson-junction arrays
summary: Series arrays of current-biased junctions coupled through a shared load map onto the Kuramoto model and phase-lock, the route to coherent microwave emission; Shapiro steps are Arnold-tongue frequency locking of a junction to an external drive.
sources: Wiesenfeld, Colet & Strogatz (1996). "Synchronization Transitions in a Disordered Josephson Series Array". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 76, 404. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.404](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.404)

name: Phonons as quantized normal modes
summary: Phonons are the quantized normal modes of the crystal's coupled harmonic oscillators; each mode contributes hbar*omega(n+1/2), giving Debye and Einstein heat capacities.

name: Normal-mode analysis behind lattice dynamics
summary: Translation symmetry turns the classical normal-mode problem of N coupled oscillators into Bloch-labelled branches, the same diagonalization used for electrons in periodic potentials.

name: Monatomic and diatomic chains to phonon branches
summary: The dispersion of a mass-spring chain is the phonon dispersion of a 1D crystal; a two-atom basis splits it into acoustic and optical branches with a gap at the zone boundary, and the dynamical matrix generalizes this to 3D.

name: Mechanical topological insulators from coupled oscillators
summary: Arrays of coupled pendula or resonators engineered to mimic a quantum spin Hall Hamiltonian show helical edge modes, demonstrating that band topology is a property of linear wave equations, not of electrons.
map: \ddot{\mathbf x}=-D\mathbf x,\ D(\mathbf k)\simeq\omega_0^2\mathbb 1+H_{\text{BHZ}}(\mathbf k);\ \omega^2\leftrightarrow E
sources: Süsstrunk & Huber (2015). "Observation of phononic helical edge states in a mechanical topological insulator". *Science* 349, 47. [doi:10.1126/science.aab0239](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab0239)

name: Drude and Lorentz models as damped driven oscillators
summary: The optical conductivity of metals (free carriers) and insulators (bound oscillators, phonons, excitons) is the response of a driven damped harmonic oscillator, with resonance width set by scattering rate.

name: Phononic crystals: Bloch bands for sound
summary: Periodic elastic composites have acoustic band structures and complete band gaps computed with Bloch's theorem, the classical-wave analogue of electronic band theory that underlies acoustic metamaterials.
map: \mathbf u(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\mathbf u(\mathbf r);\ \text{gap at }k=\pi/a\ \text{when impedance contrast }Z_1\neq Z_2
sources: Kushwaha et al. (1993). "Acoustic band structure of periodic elastic composites". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 71, 2022. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2022](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2022)

name: Josephson junction as a driven nonlinear pendulum
summary: In the RCSJ model the junction phase is a damped, driven pendulum, giving hysteresis, Shapiro steps and chaos; pumping its nonlinear inductance makes a Duffing-type parametric amplifier used for quantum-limited readout.

name: Magnetization precession as gyroscopic motion
summary: The Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation is the torque equation of a gyroscope for spin angular momentum: the magnetization precesses about the effective field and relaxes through Gilbert damping, while spin-transfer torque acts as an additional applied torque.
map: \frac{d\mathbf M}{dt}=-\gamma\mathbf M\times\mathbf H_{\text{eff}}+\frac\alpha M\mathbf M\times\frac{d\mathbf M}{dt}\leftrightarrow\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf L
sources: Gilbert (2004). "A phenomenological theory of damping in ferromagnetic materials". *IEEE Trans. Magn.* 40, 3443. [doi:10.1109/TMAG.2004.836740](https://doi.org/10.1109/TMAG.2004.836740)

name: Einstein-de Haas and Barnett effects
summary: Reversing a ferromagnet's magnetization makes the free body rotate (Einstein-de Haas), and rotating a body magnetizes it (Barnett), because total spin plus rigid-body angular momentum is conserved; these measured the electron g-factor and now enable ultrafast demagnetization studies.

name: Action-angle variables and Delaunay elements
summary: Hamilton–Jacobi theory yields Delaunay and Poincaré action-angle variables, the basis of canonical perturbation theory, averaging and Hamiltonian maps for planetary dynamics.

name: Collisionless Boltzmann equation from Liouville
summary: Liouville's theorem gives the collisionless Boltzmann equation, which underlies Jeans equations and mass estimates from stellar and galaxy dynamics, including rotation curves and velocity dispersions.

name: Phase-space density constraints on halos
summary: Liouville conservation of coarse-grained phase-space density limits how dense a halo core can be, giving Tremaine–Gunn bounds on warm and fermionic dark matter.

name: Symplectic integrators for long-term orbits
summary: Liouville's theorem and symplectic structure motivate Wisdom–Holman integrators that preserve phase-space volume and bound energy error over Gyr integrations.

name: Newtonian cosmology and minisuperspace action
summary: Friedmann equations follow from Newtonian energy conservation of a test shell, and from a minisuperspace Lagrangian in the scale factor.
breaks: Pressure gravitates and k is geometry in GR; the Newtonian derivation lacks this and fails for radiation and dark energy without ad hoc input.

name: Scalar field as particle in a potential
summary: Inflaton dynamics map to a particle rolling in a potential with Hubble friction; slow roll is the overdamped limit.
breaks: Fluctuations are quantum fields on curved space; the point-particle picture misses perturbation generation.

name: Roche potential in mass transfer
summary: The restricted three-body effective potential in a rotating frame defines Roche lobes and the L1 point, governing mass transfer and contact binaries.

name: Fermat's principle in gravitational lensing
summary: Lensing images are stationary points of the time-delay surface (geometric plus Shapiro delay), giving the lens equation and time-delay cosmography.

name: Accretion flows as viscous fluid dynamics
summary: Accretion disks around black holes are viscous shear flows, and Bondi accretion is a spherical ideal-flow solution, as in the Navier–Stokes and Euler problems.
breaks: Angular momentum transport needs MHD turbulence (MRI), not molecular viscosity, and relativity matters near the hole.

name: Shock and blast-wave hydrodynamics
summary: Sedov–Taylor and Blandford–McKee blast waves are self-similar solutions of the Euler equations, applied to GRB afterglows, supernova remnants and the shocks that accelerate cosmic rays.

name: Jeans instability and structure growth
summary: Gravitational collapse of perturbations is the Jeans instability of a self-gravitating fluid, the fluid-mechanics seed of the growth of cosmic structure, modified by expansion drag.
breaks: Dark matter is collisionless, so a fluid description holds only approximately, and nonlinear collapse needs N-body treatment.

name: Convection in stellar interiors
summary: Rayleigh–Bénard-type instability sets the Schwarzschild criterion for convection in stars, handled with mixing-length theory.
breaks: Stellar convection is highly turbulent, compressible and stratified, at huge Rayleigh numbers beyond lab regimes.

name: Dust-gas drag in disks and Stokes drag
summary: Small dust grains in protoplanetary disks couple to gas through Stokes or Epstein drag, setting stopping times and radial drift; the same viscous-drag physics governs low-Re flow.
map: t_s=\frac{m v}{F_{\rm drag}},\; F=6\pi\mu a v
breaks: Disk gas is often rarefied (Epstein regime, mean free path > grain size), unlike continuum Stokes flow.

name: Disk turbulence and angular momentum transport
summary: Turbulent viscosity (alpha prescription) drives accretion in protoplanetary disks and concentrates dust in vortices and eddies, controlling planetesimal formation.

name: Turbulent fragmentation and the IMF
summary: Supersonic turbulence in molecular clouds, with a Kolmogorov-like cascade, shapes the density distribution and fragmentation, and thus the stellar initial mass function.
breaks: Gravity, magnetic fields and feedback also matter; whether turbulence alone sets the IMF is debated.

name: MOND modifies Newtonian dynamics
summary: MOND modifies the Newtonian force law below an acceleration scale, reproducing flat rotation curves and the Tully–Fisher relation without dark matter.
breaks: Fails to account for cluster masses and CMB peaks without extra components, and needs a relativistic completion.

name: Rotation curves from Newtonian orbits
summary: Circular-orbit balance gives velocity profiles; flat curves at large radius imply M(<r) growing linearly with r, which signals dark matter.

name: Kepler orbits and precession in the Solar System
summary: Kepler problem, effective potential and perturbed-orbit precession underlie planetary and small-body orbits; secular perturbations produce apsidal and nodal precession.

name: Cluster collisions and conserved quantities
summary: Merging clusters (e.g. Bullet Cluster) are analysed with momentum and energy conservation and collision kinematics, constraining collisionless dark matter versus shocked gas.

name: Virial theorem and cluster mass
summary: Energy and momentum conservation lead to the virial theorem, used to estimate cluster dynamical masses from galaxy velocity dispersions (Zwicky's missing mass).

name: Planetary systems as few-body problems
summary: Planetary system architecture, stability and resonances are treated with the N-body problem, perturbation theory and numerical integration.

name: Lagrange points and Trojans in exoplanet systems
summary: Restricted three-body equilibria define Trojan configurations and co-orbital planets, searched for in exoplanet timing and transit data.

name: Timing and RV signals from N-body dynamics
summary: Transit-timing variations and radial-velocity multi-planet fits are inverse N-body problems; mean-motion resonances amplify TTVs, allowing masses to be inferred from perturbations.

name: Resonances and N-body Solar System evolution
summary: Mean-motion and secular resonances, symplectic N-body integrators and perturbation theory are the working tools of Solar System dynamics.

name: Coriolis force and atmospheric circulation
summary: Rotating-frame dynamics sets hot-Jupiter and terrestrial jet and wave structure, via Rossby numbers and geostrophic balance.

name: Tides and Coriolis in planetary systems
summary: Tidal forces from non-inertial frame analysis drive tidal locking, orbital migration and Roche limits; Coriolis force shapes planetary atmospheres and rotating-frame Hill dynamics.

name: Chaos in N-body stellar dynamics
summary: Exponential sensitivity in few-body encounters and cluster dynamics limits N-body predictability, so ensembles are used for population synthesis.

name: Orbits and resonances in the Galactic potential
summary: Action-angle methods and resonance structure describe stellar orbits in barred potentials; bar resonances produce moving groups and phase-space features seen in Gaia.

name: KAM tori and chaos in planetary stability
summary: Long-term stability of planetary orbits is a KAM question: resonance overlap produces chaotic zones, Kirkwood gaps and Lyapunov times of order millions of years for the Solar System.

name: Fuzzy dark matter solitons
summary: Ultralight scalar dark matter obeys a Schrödinger–Poisson system whose ground state is a stable soliton core in halos, tied to nonlinear Schrödinger structure.
breaks: Poisson coupling is nonlocal, so the system is not integrable like the cubic NLS and solitons are not exact.
